A curious mind somewhere between the laboratory,
              the chessboard, and whatever interesting thing
              I happen to discover next.

I'm a scientist in training, a problem-solver
                by nature, and a curious person by default.

I grew up in the Mtendere compound of Lusaka,
                Zambia, in a large family of nine, and I'm
                currently a junior at Grambling State University,
                studying Biology with a minor in Computer Science.

In tenth grade, I made a science project after
                just learning about acids and bases. It was a
                fire extinguisher that worked using discarded
                eggshells and ordinary vinegar, and it won me
                first place at a science fair. Since then,
                I've been excited about how "small"
                things can make a big impact on people's
                lives, and that's one of the reasons I
                chose to study Biology.

Today, I'm interested in cancer biology,
                molecular mechanisms of disease, and the
                possibility of turning scientific discoveries
                at the cellular and molecular levels into
                meaningful improvements in people's lives.

But there's more to me than coursework
                and lab work. I find my curiosity in other
                things as well. You'll probably find me
                playing basketball, studying a chess position
                (I'm a wannabe GM), listening to music,
                or getting unnecessarily competitive over Scrabble.

From studying cellular responses to environmental
              toxicants to exploring the effects of marine
              heatwaves on seabirds, these are some of the
              questions and projects I've had the chance
              to work on.

Studying how pentachlorophenol exposure affects
                  mouse liver cells, with a focus on inflammation,
                  gene expression, and cell-survival signaling.

Investigating physiological stress and oxidative
                  balance in tropical seabirds during and after
                  marine heatwave conditions in Culebra, Puerto Rico.

Led a team of five evaluating how quantum dots
                  could act as wavelength conversion materials
                  and theoretically improve solar-cell power generation.

Completed industry-led training with Memorial Sloan
                Kettering Cancer Center, Deloitte, U.S. Bank, Indeed,
                and LinkedIn, gaining exposure to professional
                communication, financial literacy, and career
                development practices.

Founded and lead the Colleges Against Cancer chapter
                at Grambling State University, building its executive
                board and organizing cancer education and fundraising
                initiatives.

Support residential students with academic,
                transitional, and social concerns while planning
                educational and community-building programs.

Mentor Zambian students pursuing higher education
                through essay reviews, SAT preparation resources,
                college application workshops, and scholarship guidance.

Some of the communities I'm part of, things I enjoy,

Studying positions, making questionable moves,

Basketball, Scrabble, Wordle, puzzles, new places,

A closer look at the research projects I've contributed
          to, the questions behind them, the methods I've learned,
          and the people I've had the opportunity to work with.

My work in the Molecular Toxicology Laboratory involves
              studying how pentachlorophenol exposure affects mouse
              liver cells. The project focuses on cellular stress,
              inflammation, and signaling mechanisms involved in
              cell survival.

I work with TIB-73 mouse liver cell cultures, maintaining
              and harvesting cells under sterile conditions. I have
              also performed molecular biology procedures, including
              SDS-PAGE and Western blotting, to examine inflammation-
              related proteins.

Through this experience and my LS-LAMP research training,
              I have developed practical experience in mammalian cell
              culture, aseptic technique, cryopreservation, PCR,
              protein analysis, and laboratory documentation.

This research investigates differences in physiological
              stress and oxidative balance in tropical seabirds from
              Culebra, Puerto Rico. The project examines three species:
              Sooty terns, White-tailed tropicbirds, and Brown noddies.

One part of the study compares samples collected during
              the 2024 El Niño period with those collected in 2025
              during La Niña conditions. The broader question is how
              changing environmental conditions may be associated
              with differences in seabird physiological health.

My laboratory work has included processing feather
              samples for corticosterone extraction and quantification,
              as well as conducting assays on bird blood plasma to
              investigate oxidative stress and antioxidant capacity.

I have also worked with ELISA, fluorescence plate-reader
              measurements, TBARS assays, and data analysis using
              Microsoft Excel and Python. These measurements provide
              different perspectives on physiological stress,
              oxidative damage, and antioxidant defenses.

A stress hormone measured in feathers to investigate
                hormonal exposure during feather growth.

An assay used to assess substances associated with
                lipid peroxidation and oxidative damage.

Stress and Condition in Relation to Diet in
                  Seabirds at Culebra, Puerto Rico.

Contrast in Condition and Stress of Tropical
                  Seabirds During and After a Marine Heat Wave.

Exploring how quantum dots could help solar cells
              capture more of the light around them.

Under Dr. Yang Haeyeon, I led a team of five in
              evaluating the potential of quantum dots as wavelength
              conversion materials for solar cells.

Using existing quantum-dot wavelength data in Microsoft
              Excel, I modeled how different quantum dots could
              influence the wavelengths of light reaching a solar cell.
              The analysis focused on cutting out wavelengths between
              620–800 nm and increasing the light available for
              absorption in the 450–500 nm range.

Through this process, we identified three quantum dots
              that were theoretically suited to these goals and
              developed a theoretical model suggesting a 2% improvement
              in power generation.

This project gave me the opportunity to work with a team,
              interpret scientific data, and explore how material
              properties could be applied to an energy challenge.
